title: In re Korean Air Lines Disaster of September 1, 1983
lead: After the destruction of Korean Air Lines Flight 007, families sought to remove a damages ceiling because the tickets’ liability notices used eight-point rather than ten-point type. Consolidation brought a second question: did each action carry its home circuit’s interpretation of federal law with it?

actors.name: Korean Air Lines
actors.role: Carrier operating Flight 007 and defendant in the wrongful-death actions

actors.name: The plaintiffs
actors.role: Wrongful-death claimants whose actions were consolidated

actors.role: District judge overseeing the consolidated pretrial proceedings

proceedings: The district court denied partial summary judgment and immediate payment on July 25, 1985. After a certified interlocutory appeal and a January 30, 1987 clarification remand, it clarified its ruling on May 7. The D.C. Circuit affirmed on September 25, 1987.
limits: This historical decision addresses the Warsaw/Montreal regime and federal-law interpretation in multidistrict litigation. It reports no individual damages judgment. Proposed legislative solutions, later Lexecon questions, and unresolved treatment after return to transferor courts are not enacted rules or additional holdings.

review.basis: Individually written and compared with the canonical full brief; no new independent opinion audit claimed.

sections.title: One disaster produces many actions
paragraphs: A Soviet aircraft shot down Korean Air Lines Flight 007 on September 1, 1983. Wrongful-death claimants sued the carrier, Korean Air Lines, and their actions were consolidated in the District of Columbia for pretrial proceedings under 28 U.S.C. § 1407, the multidistrict-litigation statute. Some actions originated in New York.

The passengers' tickets contained notice of limited liability in eight-point type. The Montreal Agreement specified ten-point type. The plaintiffs sought partial summary judgment declaring that this failure deprived Korean Air Lines of the $75,000 Warsaw/Montreal liability limit. The Second Circuit had accepted that legal argument, but Chief Judge Aubrey E. Robinson Jr., overseeing the consolidated cases, disagreed. Whether the New York actions retained the Second Circuit's interpretation could therefore affect the recoveries available in the same consolidated proceeding.

sections.title: The district judge separates a treaty from an agreement
paragraphs: Robinson examined the Warsaw Convention, which originally limited liability to approximately $8,300 subject to its defenses and exceptions, and the later Montreal Agreement. Montreal was an intercarrier special agreement, not a negotiated amendment of the treaty. It raised the limit to $75,000 and expressly waived Article 20 defenses. Although it required ten-point notice, it did not expressly make violation of that requirement a forfeiture of the damages limit.

The plaintiffs argued that inadequate notice should count as failure to deliver a ticket, invoking decisions in which nondelivery removed the limitation. Alternatively, they challenged treaty coverage because Korea had adhered to the Hague Protocol. Robinson relied on Article XXIII's adherence provision to conclude that the United States and Korea shared treaty obligations at least for the Convention's unamended portions.

For Robinson, an irregularity in a delivered ticket differed from failure to deliver a ticket. These passengers had received tickets. Decisions involving tickets delivered too late to permit insurance arrangements did not establish the same consequence for this type-size defect. Montreal's express waiver of Article 20 defenses demonstrated that a waiver could be negotiated; there was no corresponding express waiver of the liability limit. Adding one would alter the bargain that exchanged increased limits for reduced defenses.

sections.title: The ceiling survives, but payment remains disputed
paragraphs: Robinson acknowledged criticism of the aviation industry's historical protections and the appeal of full compensation. Nevertheless, courts could not rewrite a treaty maintained by the political branches. The government could enforce domestic operating requirements, including type size, without an unstated judicial sanction eliminating treaty protection. He declined the Second Circuit's ten-point bright line and held that Korean Air Lines could invoke the $75,000 limit.

The plaintiffs also requested immediate payment of $75,000. Robinson denied that request: a maximum recovery was not a guaranteed minimum, and disputes about individual damages still required resolution. His July 25, 1985 order denied partial summary judgment and immediate payment.

The district court certified an interlocutory appeal under 28 U.S.C. § 1292(b), which the D.C. Circuit permitted. Because the reach of the ruling was initially unclear, the appellate court remanded for clarification on January 30, 1987. Robinson's May 7 memorandum explained that his interpretation covered every category of consolidated action, including those from New York; he had not carved out those cases to follow Second Circuit precedent.

sources.pinpoint: District opinion, 1470–1478; clarification, 664 F. Supp. 1488–1490; appellate posture, 1172–1173

sections.title: The appellate court rejects a portable circuit rule
paragraphs: Judge Ruth Bader Ginsburg wrote for a panel also including Judges Stephen F. Williams and Douglas H. Ginsburg. All three joined the opinion and judgment. The panel expressly adopted Robinson's underlying opinion, thereby resolving the liability-limit merits as well as the transfer question.

The plaintiffs relied on Van Dusen v. Barrack, which preserved transferor state law, including choice-of-law rules, after a defendant-initiated convenience transfer of diversity litigation under § 1404(a). That rule served the Erie principle that a federal forum should not change the state-law result available where the action began. It did not give litigants an analogous entitlement to a particular circuit's understanding of one body of federal law. The panel did not decide the then-unresolved question about plaintiff-initiated transfers.

Federal venue selects a convenient location; it does not create a substantive right to a favorable federal interpretation. Each federal court must exercise its own reasoned judgment, subject to controlling appellate authority. A transferee judge should consider other circuits' decisions carefully, but those decisions do not bind it merely because an action began in those circuits. Different state laws legitimately produce variation; automatically carrying different federal interpretations into one proceeding would institutionalize inconsistency that consolidation sought to reduce. Independently reasoned uniformity, with Supreme Court review available to resolve conflicts, was preferable to mechanical repetition.

sections.title: The concurrence explores what happens on return
sections.cue: Practical concerns without a new procedural requirement
paragraphs: Douglas H. Ginsburg concurred, joined by Williams. He agreed that Van Dusen's state-law rationale did not control and found no instruction in § 1407 that a transferee judge must simulate every transferor judge's rulings. Temporary transfer conferred real authority. A specific statutory deposition provision did not imply a general origin-circuit rule. A prior determination actually precluding the parties also differed from circuit precedent that had never resolved their claims.

The difficult prospect was return of a New York case to the Second Circuit after a contrary multidistrict ruling. The concurrence acknowledged that no controlling decision had settled the interaction of circuit precedent and law of the case. It identified mitigating circumstances: many consolidated cases never return for trial, many pretrial rulings do not determine outcomes, and interlocutory review and law-of-the-case principles can reduce relitigation. Its suggestion that a dissatisfied party might need interlocutory review was a proposed solution, not an announced procedural prerequisite.

Applying every origin circuit's interpretation from the start would guarantee divergent treatment during discovery and settlement, require repeated study of many circuits, and sometimes require predictions where a circuit had not spoken. Those costs lacked the justification for respecting genuinely different state laws under Erie. The concurrence discussed legislation requiring origin-circuit law, giving multidistrict rulings effect on review elsewhere, or transferring entire cases for trial and appeal. It preferred the second over the first and identified practical costs of the third. These were recommendations, not existing statutory commands.

sources.pinpoint: Douglas H. Ginsburg concurrence, 1177–1186 and nn.2–7, 15–17

sections.title: The carrier keeps the limitation
paragraphs: The D.C. Circuit affirmed the determination that Korean Air Lines could invoke the Warsaw limitation as raised by Montreal. The decision preserved independent interpretation of federal law in the consolidated proceedings without displacing transferor state law in diversity cases.

The panel thought law-of-the-case principles should govern subsequent proceedings but expressly acknowledged that it could not conclusively settle how another court would treat the ruling after return. No individual claimant received a damages award in this decision, and no later liability or transfer outcome is supplied.
